questions.prompt: What main distinction does Chapter 9 make?
choices: It separates interest from commitment
It replaces ownership with scorekeeping
It argues that comfort should guide execution

explanation.gentle: The chapter says wanting the outcome is not the same as being committed to the work.
explanation.direct: Chapter 9 distinguishes preference-level resolve from durable commitment.
explanation.competitive: It splits liking the goal from honoring the job.

questions.prompt: Why is interest not enough by itself?
choices: Because interest always disappears immediately
Because interest weakens when the work becomes less attractive or more costly
Because commitment means never liking the result

explanation.gentle: The chapter says interest can weaken when comfort starts pushing back.
explanation.direct: Interest is unstable when the task becomes repetitive, inconvenient, or delayed in reward.
explanation.competitive: Interest likes good conditions and negotiates when the road gets ugly.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter use as the main test of resolve?
choices: Whether the goal sounds exciting in conversation
Whether comfort bargaining changes the action
Whether the reader writes longer plans

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps asking what happens when discomfort starts offering reasons to slow down.

explanation.competitive: It tests whether comfort can renegotiate the contract.

questions.prompt: Which misreading does Chapter 9 warn against?

Treating preference as weaker than commitment

Because comfort should never matter at all
